questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the columnist's argument?

options.A: The claim that the new downtown bike-lane network will reduce traffic congestion is mistaken.
options.B: The bike lanes were installed by narrowing two major car lanes.
options.C: Since the network opened, the average commute time for drivers downtown has increased by eleven percent.
options.D: The new downtown bike-lane network should be removed to restore the original car lanes.
options.E: Some people claim that the new downtown bike-lane network will reduce traffic congestion.

questions.answer: The columnist signals the main conclusion explicitly with 'But this claim is mistaken,' which rejects the cited claim that the bike lanes will reduce congestion. The two facts that follow (lanes were narrowed; commute time rose 11%) are the premises offered as evidence supporting that rejection. So the main claim is that the reduce-congestion claim is mistaken (A).

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately states the conclusion of the nutritionist's argument?

options.A: The sports drink contains added electrolytes.
options.B: The advertisement's reasoning that the drink is essential for recovery is flawed.
options.C: Plain water and a normal meal replace fluids and electrolytes for most people doing ordinary workouts.
options.D: Sports drinks should not be sold to people who do only ordinary workouts.
options.E: Drinking the sports drink after exercise is essential for recovery.

questions.answer: The phrase 'This reasoning is flawed' is the explicit conclusion indicator; it names the nutritionist's main claim, that the advertisement's argument fails. The supporting premise is that water and a meal already replace fluids and electrolytes for most people, which is why the ad's reasoning fails. Thus B is the main conclusion.

questions.stem: The main point of the editorial is that

options.A: five years ago the additional officers cost more in salaries and benefits than the extra tickets brought in.
options.B: hiring more parking-enforcement officers will increase ticket revenue.
options.C: the city council's argument that hiring more officers will pay for itself should be rejected.
options.D: the city council is generally unreliable when it comes to budget forecasts.
options.E: the city should never hire additional parking-enforcement officers under any circumstances.

questions.answer: The editorial states 'This argument should be rejected,' which is the explicit conclusion. The historical fact about the earlier trial (officers cost more than they earned) is the premise supporting that rejection. So the main point is that the council's pay-for-itself argument should be rejected (C).

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the conclusion drawn in the biologist's argument?

options.A: The decline of the songbirds in Maple Grove began three years before the pesticide was introduced.
options.B: Bird populations in nearby groves never exposed to the pesticide have fallen by similar amounts.
options.C: The pesticide is harmless to songbirds.
options.D: The suggested explanation that the new pesticide is causing the songbird decline is unconvincing.
options.E: Some other environmental factor is responsible for the songbird decline in Maple Grove.

questions.answer: 'This explanation is unconvincing' is the explicit conclusion. The two facts, that the decline predates the pesticide and that unexposed groves declined similarly, are premises showing why the pesticide explanation fails. Hence the conclusion is that the pesticide explanation is unconvincing (D).

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the manager's argument?

options.A: The company's work depends on constant client availability across five business days.
options.B: Switching all staff to a four-day workweek would not help boost the company's productivity.
options.C: Reducing coverage to four days would force the company to turn away some clients.
options.D: The colleague's proposals about scheduling are usually impractical.
options.E: The company should require staff to work more than five days per week.

questions.answer: The manager says 'I disagree that this would help us,' rejecting the colleague's claim that a four-day week would boost productivity. That rejection is the main conclusion. The points about five-day client availability and turning away clients are premises explaining why the switch would not help. So B is the conclusion.

questions.stem: The conclusion of the critic's argument is that

options.A: the studio decided to shoot the film entirely with handheld cameras.
options.B: the shaky footage makes it difficult to follow the action during crucial scenes.
options.C: the studio's decision to use handheld cameras was a mistake.
options.D: handheld cameras should never be used to shoot films.
options.E: several audience members reported feeling disoriented and nauseated while watching.

questions.answer: 'In fact, the choice was a mistake' is the critic's explicit conclusion, contradicting the studio's claim of an artistic triumph. The difficulty following the action and the reports of disorientation are premises offered as evidence that the choice was a mistake. Therefore C is the main conclusion.

questions.stem: Which one of the following conclusions follows logically from the nutritionist's statements?

options.A: The box of crackers is labeled 'organic.'
options.B: The box of crackers is not labeled 'organic.'
options.C: Any food produced without synthetic pesticides is labeled 'organic.'
options.D: If a food is not labeled 'organic,' then it was produced with synthetic pesticides.
options.E: The box of crackers is unsafe to eat.

questions.answer: The rule is: Organic-labeled → No synthetic pesticides. The crackers were produced WITH a synthetic pesticide, i.e., 'No synthetic pesticides' is false. By the contrapositive (Synthetic pesticides used → Not organic-labeled), the crackers cannot be labeled 'organic.' Choice B follows necessarily.

questions.stem: Which one of the following must be true on the basis of the statements above?

options.A: Renata is eligible to vote in the annual election.
options.B: If Renata is eligible to vote in the annual election, then she has attended at least three meetings.
options.C: If Renata has attended at least three meetings, then she is eligible to vote in the annual election.
options.D: If Renata has not attended at least three meetings, then she has not paid her dues.
options.E: Renata is not eligible to vote in the annual election.

questions.answer: 'Eligible only if X and Y' makes both paying dues AND attending three meetings necessary conditions for eligibility: Eligible → (Dues AND Three meetings). From this conditional, if Renata is eligible, then both necessary conditions hold, including attending at least three meetings. Choice B isolates one necessary condition that eligibility guarantees, and it is a valid inference.

questions.stem: Which one of the following can be properly inferred?

options.A: User K-12 enabled two-factor authentication.
options.B: User K-12 did not enable two-factor authentication.
options.C: Any user granted extended session length has enabled two-factor authentication.
options.D: If a user does not enable two-factor authentication, the system does not grant extended session length.
options.E: User K-12's account is less secure than other accounts.

questions.answer: The rule is: Two-factor enabled → Extended session granted. K-12 was NOT granted extended session length, so the necessary condition fails. By the contrapositive (Not extended session → Not two-factor enabled), K-12 did not enable two-factor authentication. Choice B follows necessarily.

questions.stem: Which one of the following can be properly inferred about the observed animal?

options.A: It is not a mammal native to the island.
options.B: It is a mammal native to the island.
options.C: It is nocturnal.
options.D: If it is nocturnal, then it is a mammal native to the island.
options.E: It is the only animal that forages near the lakeshore.

questions.answer: Two rules chain: (1) Native mammal → Nocturnal; (2) Nocturnal → Not foraging near lakeshore. Chaining gives Native mammal → Not foraging near lakeshore. The observed animal IS foraging near the lakeshore, so by the contrapositive of the chain (Foraging near lakeshore → Not a native mammal), it is not a mammal native to the island. Choice A follows necessarily.

questions.stem: Which one of the following can be properly inferred from the statement above?

options.A: If a film was produced entirely within the city limits, then it qualifies for the Heritage Production Grant.
options.B: If a film was not produced entirely within the city limits, then it does not qualify for the Heritage Production Grant.
options.C: If a film does not qualify for the Heritage Production Grant, then it was not produced entirely within the city limits.
options.D: Every film produced entirely within the city limits is eligible for some municipal grant.
options.E: Most films that qualify for the Heritage Production Grant were produced by city residents.

questions.answer: The stimulus states 'qualifies for grant -> produced within city limits' (A -> B). The only valid inference is the contrapositive: negate and flip, yielding 'not produced within city limits -> does not qualify' (not-B -> not-A). Choice B states exactly this.

questions.stem: Which one of the following follows logically from the analyst's conclusion?

options.A: If a senator received funding from the Riverside Coalition, then that senator voted for the transit bill.
options.B: If a senator did not vote for the transit bill, then that senator did not receive funding from the Riverside Coalition.
options.C: If a senator did not receive funding from the Riverside Coalition, then that senator did not vote for the transit bill.
options.D: No senator who opposed the transit bill received funding from any coalition.
options.E: The Riverside Coalition funded more senators than any other group that year.

questions.answer: The claim is 'voted for bill -> received Coalition funding' (A -> B). The contrapositive negates and flips: 'did not receive Coalition funding -> did not vote for the bill' (not-B -> not-A). Choice C matches exactly.

questions.stem: If the agronomist's statement is true, which one of the following must also be true?

options.A: If a plot's orchard yields a full apple crop, then that plot's soil is fertile.
options.B: If a plot's soil is not fertile, then that plot's orchard does not yield a full apple crop.
options.C: If a plot's orchard does not yield a full apple crop, then that plot's soil is not fertile.
options.D: A plot's orchard yields a full apple crop only if the plot receives adequate rainfall.
options.E: Fertile soil is the single most important factor in producing a full apple crop.

questions.answer: The statement is 'fertile soil -> full crop' (A -> B). The valid contrapositive negates and flips: 'no full crop -> soil not fertile' (not-B -> not-A). Choice C states exactly this.

questions.stem: Which one of the following can be properly inferred from the streaming service's terms?

options.A: Any subscriber who retains premium access for the entire year renewed before March.
options.B: Any subscriber who did not renew before March does not retain premium access for the entire year.
options.C: Any subscriber who does not retain premium access for the entire year did not renew before March.
options.D: Subscribers who renewed before March pay a lower annual rate than other subscribers.
options.E: Most subscribers who retain premium access renewed at some point during the year.

questions.answer: The term is 'renewed before March -> retains premium access' (A -> B). The contrapositive negates and flips: 'does not retain premium access -> did not renew before March' (not-B -> not-A). Choice C matches.

questions.stem: Which one of the following must be true if the manual's statement is correct?

options.A: If a compound turns the blue litmus paper red, then the compound is acidic.
options.B: If a compound is not acidic, then it does not turn the blue litmus paper red.
options.C: If a compound does not turn the blue litmus paper red, then the compound is not acidic.
options.D: A compound turns the blue litmus paper red only because of its concentration.
options.E: Acidic compounds are more common in the lab than non-acidic ones.

questions.answer: The statement is 'acidic -> turns litmus red' (A -> B). The contrapositive negates and flips: 'does not turn litmus red -> not acidic' (not-B -> not-A). Choice C states exactly this.

questions.stem: Which one of the following follows logically from the installer's explanation?

options.A: Whenever the front door is locked, the alarm is armed.
options.B: Whenever the alarm is not armed, the front door is not locked.
options.C: Whenever the front door is not locked, the alarm is not armed.
options.D: The front door cannot be locked unless the homeowner is present.
options.E: Arming the alarm is the most effective way to keep the front door secure.

questions.answer: The statement is 'alarm armed -> front door locked' (A -> B). The contrapositive negates and flips: 'front door not locked -> alarm not armed' (not-B -> not-A). Choice C states this exactly.

questions.stem: If the statements above are true, then which one of the following must also be true?

options.A: Most retired teachers have completed the advanced inventory-management course.
options.B: At least one retired teacher has completed the advanced inventory-management course.
options.C: Most volunteers who have completed the advanced inventory-management course are retired teachers.
options.D: All volunteers who are retired teachers have completed the advanced inventory-management course.
options.E: Most people who have completed the advanced inventory-management course volunteer at the Hawthorne food bank.

questions.answer: Both 'most' statements range over the same group: the volunteers at the food bank. Since a majority of the volunteers are retired teachers and a majority have completed the course, these two majorities must overlap (any two subsets each comprising more than half of the same finite set share at least one member). Therefore at least one volunteer is both a retired teacher and a course-completer, which guarantees that at least one retired teacher has completed the course. (B) states exactly this minimal guaranteed overlap.

questions.stem: Which one of the following can be properly inferred from the botanist's statements?

options.A: Most of the orchids in the greenhouse are at serious risk of dying within the month.
options.B: At least one orchid in the greenhouse is at serious risk of dying within the month.
options.C: Every flowering orchid in the greenhouse is infected with the rust fungus.
options.D: Most of the orchids at serious risk of dying are flowering.
options.E: Most flowering orchids are infected with the rust fungus.

questions.answer: Among the orchids in this one greenhouse, the majority that are flowering and the majority that are infected must overlap in at least one orchid (two subsets each larger than half of the same finite set necessarily share a member). That at-least-one orchid is both flowering and infected, and the third premise says any such plant is at serious risk of dying within the month. So at least one orchid is at serious risk, which is exactly (B).

questions.stem: If the editorial's statements are true, which one of the following must also be true?

options.A: Some novels published by independent presses were written by debut authors.
options.B: Most novels published by independent presses were written by debut authors.
options.C: Every novel written by a debut author this year was published by an independent press.
options.D: Some novels written by debut authors were not published by independent presses.
options.E: All novels written by debut authors were shortlisted for the Brennan Prize.

questions.answer: The shortlisted debut-author novels exist (the second premise asserts 'some'), and every shortlisted novel was published by an independent press (first premise). So those particular debut-author novels are also independent-press novels. That gives us at least one novel that is both independent-press-published and written by a debut author, which is exactly the 'some' claim in (A). This is the valid combination of a universal ('all shortlisted are X') with an existential ('some shortlisted are Y').

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the two premises (setting aside the analyst's further conclusion)?

options.A: Some patients over sixty in the trial responded well to the drug.
options.B: Most patients who responded well to the drug were over sixty.
options.C: Patients over sixty responded better to the drug than younger patients did.
options.D: Most patients over sixty respond well to this drug.
options.E: Some patients who responded well to the drug were under sixty.

questions.answer: Both premises range over the same group, the trial enrollees. A majority responded well and a majority were over sixty, so these two majorities must overlap in at least one enrollee. That enrollee is both over sixty and a good responder, establishing that some over-sixty patients responded well. (A) states precisely this guaranteed overlap and nothing more.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes what can and cannot be validly inferred from the two factual claims in the note?

options.A: It can be validly inferred that some teaching assistants have published a peer-reviewed article, but not that most of them have.
options.B: It can be validly inferred that most teaching assistants have published a peer-reviewed article.
options.C: It can be validly inferred that most published graduate students are teaching assistants, but not the reverse.
options.D: Neither that some nor that any teaching assistants have published can be validly inferred.
options.E: It can be validly inferred that all teaching assistants who have published are graduate students, and nothing more.

questions.answer: Both 'most' claims range over the same set, the department's graduate students, so the majority who have published and the majority who are teaching assistants must share at least one member. That guarantees 'some teaching assistants have published.' But two overlapping majorities guarantee only a single shared member, not that a majority of the TAs have published, so the stronger 'most TAs have published' does not follow. (A) captures both halves: 'some' is valid, 'most' is not.

questions.stem: The argument depends on assuming which one of the following?

options.A: The bike-share program is the most cost-effective method the city could have used to reduce automobile traffic downtown.
options.B: At least some of the additional bicycles seen downtown are being ridden by people who would otherwise have driven.
options.C: Most residents who use the bike-share program had never ridden a bicycle downtown before the program launched.
options.D: The number of automobiles on downtown streets has decreased since the bike-share program launched.
options.E: Cycling downtown is safer now than it was before the bike-share program launched.

questions.answer: The conclusion is that the program persuaded residents to give up driving in favor of cycling. The evidence is only that more bicycles are present. For the leap from 'more bikes' to 'people switched from driving' to hold, at least some of those extra riders must be former (or would-be) drivers rather than, say, former pedestrians, bus riders, or tourists. Negate B: if NONE of the additional cyclists would otherwise have driven, then the program persuaded no one to give up driving, and the conclusion collapses. That makes B a necessary assumption.

questions.stem: The nutritionist's argument relies on assuming which one of the following?

options.A: People who skip breakfast consume more total calories per day than people who eat breakfast.
options.B: Eating breakfast, rather than some other factor associated with eating breakfast, is at least part of what accounts for the lower average weight of breakfast eaters.
options.C: The study included a representative sample of both breakfast eaters and breakfast skippers.
options.D: No food other than breakfast has any effect on a person's weight.
options.E: People who eat breakfast every morning will lose weight more quickly than people who eat breakfast only occasionally.

questions.answer: The argument moves from a correlation (breakfast eaters weigh less) to a prescription (eat breakfast to lose weight). That move only works if eating breakfast itself contributes to the lower weight, rather than the correlation being entirely explained by some third factor (e.g., breakfast eaters happen to exercise more or be more health-conscious overall). Negate B: if eating breakfast contributes nothing and the entire association is due to other factors, then adopting breakfast would do nothing for weight loss, and the recommendation has no support. So B is the assumption bridging correlation to causation.

questions.stem: The editorial's reasoning depends on which one of the following assumptions?

options.A: The discount retail store would sell goods at lower prices than any locally owned shop in town currently offers.
options.B: Most visitors come to the town primarily because of its locally owned shops.
options.C: Preserving the town's attractiveness to visitors is a more important goal than providing residents with low-priced goods.
options.D: If the locally owned shops were to close for some reason other than competition, the town's distinctive character would be unaffected.
options.E: No new locally owned shops would open to replace those driven out of business by the discount store.

questions.answer: The chain is: discount store opens, leads to local shops closing, which leads to loss of distinctive character, so reject the store. The step from 'this store drives local shops out of business' to 'the town loses its distinctive character' assumes the loss is net and lasting, i.e., that the closed shops are not replaced by other locally owned shops that would preserve the same character. Negate E: if new locally owned shops would open to replace the closed ones, then the town would retain its distinctive character and the argument's predicted harm evaporates. So E is necessary.

questions.stem: The manager's argument assumes which one of the following?

options.A: Releasing software weekly does not introduce additional costs that outweigh the savings from catching bugs sooner.
options.B: Bugs found during testing are always cheaper to fix than bugs found by customers after release.
options.C: The development team currently spends more on fixing bugs than on any other single activity.
options.D: Weekly releases contain, on average, exactly one-quarter as many changes as monthly releases.
options.E: No team that releases monthly has ever caught a bug as early as a team that releases weekly.

questions.answer: The conclusion is a recommendation to switch to weekly releases, supported by the claim that doing so saves money by catching bugs earlier. But a recommendation grounded in 'it saves money' requires that the change not also create offsetting costs (e.g., the overhead of preparing and deploying four times as many releases). Negate A: if weekly releases introduce extra costs that exceed the bug-catching savings, then switching would not save money on net, and the recommendation loses its support. So A is a required assumption.

questions.stem: The archaeologist's conclusion depends on the assumption that

options.A: the decorative patterns on the pottery were considered valuable by the people of both settlements
options.B: the similarity in decorative patterns is not better explained by some factor other than regular trade between the two settlements
options.C: the northern settlement was the original source of the decorative patterns found at both sites
options.D: the two settlements existed during the same historical period
options.E: no other settlements in the region produced pottery with these decorative patterns

questions.answer: The argument infers regular trade from a similarity in pottery patterns. That inference holds only if the similarity is actually best accounted for by regular trade rather than by an alternative explanation (shared cultural tradition, a common third-party supplier, independent invention, migration, etc.). Negate B: if the similarity IS better explained by some other factor, then it provides no support for the trade conclusion. Ruling out a better competing explanation is exactly the gap the argument must close, making B necessary.

questions.stem: The columnist's argument relies on assuming which one of the following?

options.A: Requiring students to own laptops will impose a significant financial burden on some incoming students.
options.B: The university has tried other policies in the past that failed to raise students' grades.
options.C: Owning a laptop is not itself a cause of the higher grades earned by students who currently own laptops.
options.D: Students who own laptops use them primarily for purposes unrelated to their coursework.
options.E: The grades of students who own laptops are higher than the grades of any students who do not own laptops.

questions.answer: The columnist argues the policy will NOT raise grades, attacking the administrators' correlation-based reasoning. For the columnist to be right that mandating laptops won't help, the higher grades of current laptop owners must not actually be caused by laptop ownership; instead the correlation must stem from something else (e.g., wealthier or more motivated students both own laptops and study more). Negate C: if owning a laptop IS a cause of higher grades, then requiring everyone to own one could plausibly raise grades, undermining the columnist's conclusion. So C is necessary to the columnist's position.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the council member's argument?

options.A: The proposed bicycle-lane network should be approved.
options.B: Constructing the bicycle-lane network will require temporarily closing several busy streets.
options.C: The temporary street closures will frustrate commuters for only a few months.
options.D: Once built, the bicycle lanes will reduce traffic congestion and pollution for decades.
options.E: A short-lived inconvenience is a small price to pay for lasting benefits.

questions.answer: The council member is responding to colleagues who want to reject the network. Every other statement (the closures are brief, the benefits last decades, the trade-off is worth it) functions as support for a single recommendation. The word 'therefore' explicitly flags that recommendation: 'We should therefore approve the network.' That is the claim everything else is marshaled to support, so (A) is the main conclusion.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main conclusion of the columnist's argument?

options.A: Late-night eaters in the studies consumed substantially more total calories than early eaters did.
options.B: The popular claim that late-night eating itself causes weight gain is based on a misinterpretation of the evidence.
options.C: The timing of one's meals has no measurable effect on body weight.
options.D: Studies have shown that late-night eaters gained more weight than early eaters.
options.E: People who wish to lose weight should focus on total calorie intake rather than meal timing.

questions.answer: The argument's purpose is to debunk a popular claim. The findings about equal weight after controlling for calories, and the calorie difference between groups, are evidence. The columnist's verdict on the fad is the final sentence: the claim 'rests on a misreading of the evidence.' Choice (B) restates exactly that evaluative conclusion about the popular claim.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the historian's argument?

options.A: Literacy rates rose dramatically only in regions that already had networks of parish schools.
options.B: The printing press did little to increase literacy where parish schools were absent.
options.C: It is commonly believed that the printing press single-handedly caused the spread of literacy.
options.D: Rather than being the true cause of rising literacy, the printing press amplified gains already made possible by schooling.
options.E: Parish schools were responsible for all of the literacy gains seen in early modern Europe.

questions.answer: The historian challenges a common belief that the press caused literacy. The regional evidence (gains only where schools existed; little effect without schools) supports the corrective claim in the last sentence: the press was not the true engine but an amplifier of school-driven gains. That corrective claim, signaled by 'then' and 'rather,' is what everything else supports, making (D) the main point.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the conclusion of the manager's argument?

options.A: Adopting the new testing tool would require weeks of training.
options.B: The current manual process already catches the vast majority of serious defects before release.
options.C: The company should retain its current testing process for the time being.
options.D: The new tool would provide only a modest improvement in early bug detection.
options.E: The disruption caused by adopting the new tool would outweigh its benefits.

questions.answer: The manager is deciding between adopting a new tool and keeping the current one. The training cost, the effectiveness of the current process, and the cost-benefit judgment are all reasons. They converge on the recommendation in the final sentence: keep the current process for now. That recommended action is the conclusion, so (C) is correct.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main conclusion of the astronomer's argument?

options.A: Space telescopes avoid the image blurring caused by Earth's atmosphere.
options.B: Ground-based telescopes can be built larger and serviced more easily than orbiting telescopes.
options.C: New techniques can sharpen ground-based images to nearly the clarity of space-telescope images.
options.D: It would be a mistake to cut funding for ground-based telescopes.
options.E: Space telescopes are no better than ground-based telescopes in any respect.

questions.answer: The astronomer opposes commentators who want to defund ground-based telescopes. The points about size, serviceability, and new sharpening techniques are reasons that the funding cut is unwarranted. The 'therefore' sentence states the conclusion: cutting their funding would be a mistake. (D) restates that exact judgment.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the critic's argument?

options.A: Reviewers have praised the novel's intricate plot as its greatest achievement.
options.B: A plot, however clever, is merely scaffolding for a novel.
options.C: The novel's real achievement lies in its vividly drawn protagonist rather than in its plot.
options.D: Readers tend to remember a novel's characters long after they have forgotten its plot.
options.E: The novel's protagonist lingers in the reader's mind long after the plot's twists have faded.

questions.answer: The critic explicitly disagrees with reviewers who credit the plot. The general claim that plot is mere scaffolding, the observation that characters are what readers remember, and the memorable protagonist are all reasons supporting the critic's contrary verdict. The final sentence states that verdict: the book's true accomplishment lies in the protagonist, not the plot. (C) captures it.

questions.stem: The claim that lower travel times attract additional drivers who had previously avoided the route plays which one of the following roles in the columnist's argument?

options.A: It is the main conclusion that the columnist is attempting to establish.
options.B: It is a premise offered in support of the columnist's conclusion that the expansion will not provide lasting relief.
options.C: It is a position that the columnist rejects as inconsistent with the available evidence.
options.D: It is an intermediate conclusion drawn from the claim that city planners favor adding lanes.
options.E: It states the prediction made by the city planners that the columnist sets out to evaluate.

questions.answer: The columnist's main conclusion is that the expansion will not provide lasting relief (signaled by 'therefore'). The claim about lower travel times attracting drivers is part of the documented pattern offered as evidence (a premise) for that conclusion. It explains the mechanism by which added capacity fails to reduce congestion, supporting the conclusion.

questions.stem: The claim that transparency can sometimes discourage self-dealing among public officials plays which one of the following roles in the editorial's argument?

options.A: It is the primary conclusion the editorial seeks to support.
options.B: It is a consideration the editorial concedes before arguing that it is outweighed by other factors.
options.C: It is evidence offered directly in support of rejecting the proposal.
options.D: It is a claim the editorial argues is factually false.
options.E: It is an assumption required for the supporters' argument to be valid.

questions.answer: The phrase 'It is true that... Nevertheless' marks a concession: the editorial grants that transparency can discourage self-dealing, then pivots to reasons this benefit does not apply here (no large budget) and is outweighed (deterring qualified candidates). The conceded point is acknowledged as valid but set aside, which is the textbook structure of a concession.

questions.stem: The statement that participants gained the same amount of weight whether their largest meal came at noon or near midnight figures in the nutritionist's argument in which one of the following ways?

options.A: It is the conclusion that the nutritionist draws about meal timing and weight.
options.B: It is experimental evidence used to support the nutritionist's conclusion about what determines weight gain.
options.C: It is a claim made by the diet guides that the nutritionist sets out to defend.
options.D: It is a generalization for which the controlled studies are offered as counterexamples.
options.E: It restates the nutritionist's recommendation about how readers should plan their meals.

questions.answer: The study result that participants gained the same weight regardless of meal timing is the empirical evidence (premise). The conclusion, signaled by 'So,' is that meal timing by itself does not determine weight gain and that total calories matter. The study finding supports that conclusion.

questions.stem: The astronomer's statement that comet swarms can produce irregular dips in a star's brightness serves which one of the following functions in the argument?

options.A: It is the main conclusion the astronomer defends about the cause of the dimming.
options.B: It is a point the astronomer grants while maintaining that it does not fit the observed pattern.
options.C: It is the premise from which the astronomer concludes that a planet is transiting the star.
options.D: It is a hypothesis the astronomer shows to be internally contradictory.
options.E: It is offered as the strongest available objection to the colleague's comet-swarm explanation.

questions.answer: Signaled by 'Admittedly... But,' the astronomer concedes that comet swarms can cause irregular dimming, then argues this does not match the observed regular, precisely periodic dimming. The concession grants the colleague a point before showing it is inapplicable, which is the role of a concession.

questions.stem: The claim that other factors surely influenced those outcomes plays which one of the following roles in the economist's argument?

options.A: It is the main conclusion of the economist's argument.
options.B: It is an acknowledgment of a limitation in the economist's evidence, offered before the economist draws a conclusion from that evidence anyway.
options.C: It is the prediction made by the critics that the economist aims to discredit.
options.D: It is the primary evidence the economist uses to reject the critics' prediction.
options.E: It is an assumption without which the economist's conclusion could not follow.

questions.answer: The economist's evidence is the employment rise in neighboring states; the conclusion is that this gives little reason to expect widespread layoffs. The 'While other factors surely influenced those outcomes' clause concedes a limitation of that evidence (the rise might be due to other factors), yet the economist proceeds to draw the conclusion. It is a concession acknowledging a weakness before reasoning past it.

questions.stem: The statement that literacy remained low for generations in regions that had presses but lacked parish schools plays which one of the following roles in the historian's argument?

options.A: It is the overall conclusion that the historian's argument is designed to support.
options.B: It is evidence that the historian uses to argue against the view that the press single-handedly caused the spread of literacy.
options.C: It is the common view about the printing press that the historian ultimately endorses.
options.D: It is a concession the historian makes to the position being criticized.
options.E: It is an objection to the historian's claim that schooling drove the rise in literacy.

questions.answer: The historian opposes the view that the press alone caused literacy's spread. The observation that regions with presses but no schools stayed illiterate is evidence (a premise) against the press-alone view: if the press were sufficient, those regions should have become literate too. It supports the conclusion that schooling, not the press alone, drove the change.

questions.stem: The nutritionist's argument proceeds by

options.A: offering an alternative explanation for an observed correlation in order to undermine a proposed causal claim
options.B: presenting a counterexample that directly contradicts the study's reported findings
options.C: questioning the methods used to gather the data on which a conclusion is based
options.D: appealing to expert consensus to reject a popular but mistaken belief
options.E: demonstrating that the correlation reported in the study does not actually exist

questions.answer: The nutritionist accepts the observed correlation (breakfast-eaters weigh less) but challenges the causal conclusion drawn from it (that eating breakfast prevents weight gain). The mechanism is to supply a different explanation for that correlation: skippers are disproportionately dieters who tend to regain weight, so dieting status, not breakfast-skipping, may drive the weight difference. Offering an alternative cause for a correlation in order to defeat a causal claim is precisely the move described in A.

questions.stem: The critic responds to the defenders' argument by

options.A: arguing that the defenders' principle, if accepted, would lead to a conclusion they would reject
options.B: offering evidence that Da Souza is not in fact the greatest sculptor of the generation
options.C: showing that the defenders have contradicted an earlier claim they made
options.D: pointing out that the defenders have provided no definition of the term 'masterpiece'
options.E: establishing that the sculpture in question is actually a failure

questions.answer: The defenders' reasoning is: this work is a masterpiece because its creator is the greatest sculptor. The critic generalizes that principle (merit follows from creator's reputation) and shows it entails that acclaimed artists could never produce failures, an implication the defenders themselves would call absurd. This is a reductio: take the opponent's principle, draw out an unacceptable consequence, and thereby reject the principle. That is exactly A.

questions.stem: The economist counters the opponent's claim primarily by

options.A: citing a case whose outcome is difficult to reconcile with the opponent's prediction
options.B: showing that the opponent's argument relies on an undefined key term
options.C: proposing a compromise position acceptable to both sides of the dispute
options.D: arguing that the opponent is not qualified to make economic predictions
options.E: establishing that raising the minimum wage always increases employment

questions.answer: The opponent predicts that raising the minimum wage causes widespread job losses. The economist points to Brightport, a real case where a large minimum-wage increase was followed by a slight rise, not a fall, in low-wage employment. That outcome is hard to square with the opponent's prediction, so it functions as disconfirming evidence against the causal claim. Using a case that conflicts with a prediction to undercut it is exactly A.

questions.stem: The columnist's argument proceeds by

options.A: showing that a principle underlying the mayor's reasoning would, if applied consistently, rule out projects the mayor presumably accepts
options.B: presenting statistical evidence that the bridge would not in fact be expensive
options.C: conceding the mayor's conclusion while disputing the reasons offered for it
options.D: attacking the mayor's character rather than the substance of the mayor's argument
options.E: proving that the new bridge would generate more benefits than it would cost

questions.answer: The mayor's stated reason is 'it would be expensive.' The columnist extracts the underlying principle, do not undertake expensive projects, and shows that applied consistently it would bar roads and hospitals too, projects the mayor presumably supports. Demonstrating that an opponent's principle, applied consistently, generates conclusions the opponent rejects is the reductio-style move described in A.

questions.stem: The archaeologist's argument proceeds by

options.A: contending that the evidence offered for a hypothesis is equally consistent with a competing hypothesis
options.B: presenting newly discovered evidence that decisively establishes the true cause of the abandonment
options.C: arguing that the colleague has misidentified the type of sediment found at the site
options.D: showing that the colleague's hypothesis is internally contradictory
options.E: concluding that the settlement at Tarsk was never actually abandoned

questions.answer: The colleague infers drought-caused abandonment from a dry sediment layer. The archaeologist argues that this same sediment layer would appear under a rival scenario (people left for unrelated reasons, then windblown dust accumulated). Because the evidence fits both the drought hypothesis and the competing one, it fails to support the drought hypothesis specifically. Showing that the cited evidence is equally consistent with a competing hypothesis is exactly A.

questions.stem: The editor responds to the readers' complaint by

options.A: drawing a distinction between two things the readers have treated as the same
options.B: denying that the newspaper ever endorsed the candidate in question
options.C: providing examples of unbiased reporting from the newspaper's news pages
options.D: arguing that all newspapers are entitled to express political opinions
options.E: conceding that the news coverage has in fact been biased

questions.answer: The readers equate an editorial endorsement with bias in coverage. The editor's whole move is to separate two things: bias means slanting factual reporting, whereas an editorial endorsement is an openly labeled opinion. By distinguishing the labeled opinion from biased reporting, the editor shows the readers have conflated distinct things. Drawing a distinction between two conflated things is exactly A.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the administrator's argument?

options.A: The alcohol-based foam is somewhat more expensive per application than the antibacterial soap it replaced.
options.B: During the same six-month period, the hospital made no other changes to its surgical procedures, equipment, or sterilization practices.
options.C: Some surgeons at the hospital reported that the new foam dried their hands less than the old soap did.
options.D: At a different hospital, switching to the same alcohol-based foam did not reduce post-surgical infection rates.
options.E: The antibacterial soap had been used at the hospital for more than fifteen years before the switch.

questions.answer: The argument infers that the foam caused the drop in infections. The central vulnerability is that some OTHER change during the six months could explain the decline. By establishing that no other changes were made to procedures, equipment, or sterilization, choice B rules out the most prominent alternative causes and ties the infection drop more tightly to the one variable that did change (the foam). This narrows the gap between the premise (infections fell after the switch) and the conclusion (the foam is more effective).

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the columnist's argument?

options.A: Birch Road and Elm Avenue carry roughly the same volume of nighttime traffic.
options.B: The number of daytime accidents on Birch Road remained constant over the same period.
options.C: Traffic volume on Birch Road did not increase in the year after the streetlights were installed.
options.D: Some drivers report feeling safer on well-lit roads than on poorly lit ones.
options.E: The streetlights installed on Birch Road were among the brightest available models.

questions.answer: The columnist's evidence is the Birch Road case: lights went up, yet accidents rose. The obvious objection is that something else (such as a surge in how many cars used the road) caused the rise in accidents, leaving the lighting's true effect masked. Choice C closes that gap by ruling out increased traffic volume as the explanation for the accident increase, making it more plausible that the lights themselves failed to help. This supports the inference from the single example to the general claim.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the nutritionist's argument?

options.A: Large breakfasts are typically higher in protein than other meals eaten during the day.
options.B: People who skip breakfast often report feeling unusually hungry by late morning.
options.C: When habitual breakfast-skippers were assigned to begin eating a large breakfast, their total daily calorie intake decreased.
options.D: Many people who eat a large breakfast also exercise regularly.
options.E: People who eat a large breakfast tend to weigh less than people who skip breakfast.

questions.answer: The argument leaps from a correlation (big-breakfast eaters consume fewer total calories) to a causal recommendation (eating a big breakfast will MAKE you eat less). The gap is the classic correlation-causation gap: perhaps people who naturally eat less just happen to eat big breakfasts. Choice C provides experimental evidence: when skippers were made to eat a large breakfast, their intake actually fell. This directly supports that the breakfast causes the reduction, closing the gap.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the archaeologist's argument?

options.A: The decorative patterns at both sites are far more elaborate than those found at any other known site in the region.
options.B: Chemical analysis shows that the clay in the Tola shards came from a deposit located near the Keman site.
options.C: The rugged terrain between the two sites can be crossed on foot in about two weeks.
options.D: Pottery from the Keman site has been dated to roughly the same period as the pottery from the Tola site.
options.E: Neither community is known to have had contact with any third community that produced similar patterns.

questions.answer: The conclusion is that the matching patterns resulted from direct trade between the two communities. A leading alternative is that the two communities independently developed similar patterns, or that the resemblance is coincidental. Choice B provides physical evidence of actual movement of goods: the clay in Tola's pottery originated near Keman, meaning the pots themselves (or their material) traveled between the sites. That is direct support for trade, sharply narrowing the gap.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the editorial's argument?

options.A: The standardized math tests are designed to measure a broad range of mathematical reasoning skills.
options.B: Students who participate in the music program also tend to enjoy attending school more than non-participants do.
options.C: Among students with similar prior math achievement, those who later joined the music program went on to outscore those who did not.
options.D: Music programs in other cities have proven popular with both students and parents.
options.E: The after-school music program is less expensive to run than most other after-school enrichment programs.

questions.answer: The argument concludes that music training causes higher math scores. The obvious confound is self-selection: students who join music programs may already be stronger at math (or come from more advantaged backgrounds), so the score gap could predate any music training. Choice C controls for prior math achievement by comparing students who started out equally and showing the music participants pulled ahead afterward. This isolates the program as the likely cause, directly narrowing the premise-to-conclusion gap.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the officials' argument?

options.A: The LED streetlights installed on Maple Avenue consume substantially less electricity than the older streetlights they replaced.
options.B: During the same three-year period, the city lowered the nighttime speed limit on Maple Avenue and added several speed-enforcement cameras there.
options.C: A few residents living along Maple Avenue have complained that the new LED streetlights are too bright and disrupt their sleep.
options.D: Some major avenues in the city already have lighting that is nearly as bright as the new LED streetlights on Maple Avenue.
options.E: Daytime traffic accidents on Maple Avenue remained roughly constant over the three-year period.

questions.answer: The argument assumes the brighter lighting caused the drop in nighttime accidents. (B) supplies an alternative explanation: a lower nighttime speed limit plus new enforcement cameras were introduced on the same street during the same window, and these measures plausibly account for the accident decline. This undercuts the causal claim that the lighting was responsible, and therefore weakens the inference that installing the lights elsewhere would reduce accidents.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the columnist's argument?

options.A: The survey included roughly equal numbers of men and women across a wide range of ages.
options.B: Some people who skip breakfast report feeling more energetic in the late morning than they did when they ate breakfast.
options.C: People who are already overweight are far more likely than others to skip breakfast as a deliberate strategy to cut calories.
options.D: Many nutritionists recommend that breakfast include protein and whole grains rather than sugary cereals.
options.E: On average, people who eat breakfast consume slightly more total calories per day than people who skip it.

questions.answer: The argument treats a correlation (breakfast-eaters weigh less) as proof that eating breakfast prevents weight gain. (C) reverses the causal direction: being overweight causes people to skip breakfast, rather than skipping breakfast causing higher weight. If overweight people deliberately skip breakfast to lose weight, that fully explains the correlation without breakfast having any preventive effect, gutting the columnist's causal claim.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the editorial's argument?

options.A: Crestwood State spends considerably less per student on education than our state does, and faces far higher rates of student poverty.
options.B: Teachers in Crestwood State are paid, on average, slightly more than teachers in our state.
options.C: Most teachers in our state already intended to pursue a master's degree even before the new requirement.
options.D: Requiring a master's degree increases the cost of becoming a teacher, which may discourage some people from entering the profession.
options.E: Test scores are only one of several measures that education researchers use to assess student outcomes.

questions.answer: The editorial assumes Crestwood is comparable to the author's state, so that equal test scores show the requirement does no good. (A) breaks that comparison: Crestwood has much higher poverty and far less funding, factors that depress test scores. If the requirement were actually raising Crestwood's scores against those headwinds, scores could still end up merely equal to the author's state, meaning the requirement may well help. This alternative explanation undermines the editorial's inference that equal scores prove the requirement is ineffective.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the wellness director's argument?

options.A: Standing desks are considerably more expensive than the traditional sitting desks the company currently uses.
options.B: The standing desks were given first to employees who had specifically requested them because they had previously found that standing relieved their existing back pain.
options.C: A few employees who switched to standing desks have reported new discomfort in their feet and knees.
options.D: Some competing companies in the same industry have also begun providing standing desks to their employees.
options.E: Employees who use standing desks take roughly the same number of sick days as employees who use sitting desks.

questions.answer: The argument assumes the standing desks caused the lower back-pain rates, so giving them to everyone will reduce pain. (B) reveals a selection effect: the standing desks went to people who already knew standing relieved their back pain. These employees were predisposed to report less pain regardless of any general causal effect, so the comparison is confounded. This undercuts the inference that standing desks would help the remaining employees, who were not self-selected.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the archaeologist's argument?

options.A: Several other settlements from the same period in the region have yielded the remains of bronze-working furnaces.
options.B: The bronze tools found at Tarn show signs of having been repaired and resharpened many times over many years.
options.C: Metalworking at the time was typically carried out in a dedicated area set well apart from a settlement's living quarters, and the surrounding land beyond Tarn has never been excavated.
options.D: The chemical composition of the bronze tools at Tarn closely matches that of bronze artifacts found at settlements hundreds of miles away.
options.E: Bronze tools were highly valued in the period and were often passed down within families for several generations.

questions.answer: The argument assumes that because no metalworking debris was found at the site, the people of Tarn could not have made the tools, so they must have traded for them. (C) attacks that assumption: metalworking was normally done in a separate area apart from living quarters, and the land beyond Tarn has never been dug up. The absence of furnace evidence within the excavated settlement is therefore unsurprising even if the people did make their own tools, so the absence does not support the trade conclusion.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most weakens the manager's argument?

options.A: The cost of redesigning the mobile app would be significantly higher than the cost of redesigning the website was.
options.B: A small number of longtime customers complained that they had trouble finding familiar features on the redesigned website.
options.C: The redesigned website launched at the start of the company's busiest seasonal shopping period, during which its sales rise sharply every year.
options.D: Most of the company's customers who use the website also use its mobile app.
options.E: Several of the company's competitors redesigned their own websites during the same quarter.

questions.answer: The argument assumes the redesign caused the 18 percent sales increase. (C) provides an alternative explanation: the redesign launched at the start of a seasonal shopping period when sales jump every year anyway. The increase may therefore be due to the predictable seasonal surge rather than the redesign, undercutting the claim that the redesign was responsible and thus the inference that redesigning the app would similarly boost sales.

questions.stem: The reasoning in the department's report is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

options.A: treats the absence of evidence that morale is good as positive evidence that morale is poor
options.B: generalizes about all employees from a group of respondents who selected themselves into the survey and so may not be representative of the workforce
options.C: overlooks the possibility that morale, even if poor now, could improve in the near future
options.D: assumes that because most respondents share an opinion, that opinion must be correct
options.E: fails to consider whether senior management's morale differs from that of ordinary employees

questions.answer: The survey was voluntary and self-selected: only employees who chose to respond did so, and just 300 of 4,000 participated. People with strong grievances are disproportionately motivated to answer a morale survey, so the 78 percent figure cannot be safely projected onto the whole workforce. This is the textbook unrepresentative-sample (self-selection) flaw, which (B) states precisely.

questions.stem: The argument against Senator Alvarez's claim is flawed because it

options.A: presumes, without justification, that anyone who profits from a regulation must have proposed it dishonestly
options.B: rejects the senator's claim merely by pointing to her financial interest, rather than addressing whether the claim itself is true
options.C: treats the failure to prove that the current rules are adequate as proof that they are inadequate
options.D: relies on the testimony of a person who is not an acknowledged expert on commercial fishing safety
options.E: confuses the question of whether the bill should pass with the question of who would benefit from it

questions.answer: The argument dismisses Alvarez's factual claim (that current rules are inadequate) solely by citing her financial stake in safety-equipment manufacturing. Her potential conflict of interest gives a motive but says nothing about whether the rules actually are inadequate. Attacking the source rather than the substance of the claim is the ad hominem (circumstantial) flaw, captured exactly by (B).

questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because it

options.A: relies on testimony about the editor's character from sources whose reliability is not established
options.B: trades on two different senses of a key term, using 'free' to mean politically unconstrained in one place and personally unconstrained in another
options.C: infers that because something is true of a society as a whole, it must be true of each individual within that society
options.D: assumes that a magazine's editorial stance is determined entirely by the personality of its editor-in-chief
options.E: takes for granted that defending a right in print is the same as exercising that right

questions.answer: The word 'free' shifts meaning. The first sentence uses 'free society' in a political sense (a society that tolerates open criticism of government). The description of the editor as a 'free spirit' uses 'free' in a personal-temperament sense (someone who dislikes constraints and taking orders). The argument links the two only because the same word appears, concluding she will champion the political freedom to criticize government. That is equivocation, stated by (B).

questions.stem: The commissioner's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it

options.A: fails to consider that cameras might reduce collisions at some intersections while increasing them at others
options.B: overlooks the possibility that intersections are selected for cameras precisely when their collision counts are unusually high, so that a subsequent decline may reflect a return to typical levels rather than any effect of the cameras
options.C: assumes that the only way to reduce collisions at an intersection is to install a traffic camera there
options.D: ignores the costs of installing and maintaining cameras at fifty separate intersections
options.E: treats a reduction in reported collisions as equivalent to a reduction in actual collisions

questions.answer: Cameras are installed where collisions are high, and the plan even targets the fifty highest-rate intersections. An intersection whose count is unusually high one year tends to fall toward its normal level the next year regardless of any intervention (regression to the mean). The commissioner attributes the post-installation drop to the cameras while overlooking this selection-driven artifact. (B) names this alternative-cause/regression flaw precisely.

questions.stem: The critic's reasoning is most vulnerable to the criticism that it

options.A: concludes that a claim is false merely because the argument given for it is inadequate
options.B: rejects the museum's conclusion on the basis of considerations that are irrelevant to how popular the exhibit is
options.C: assumes that ticket sales are never a reliable measure of an exhibit's popularity
options.D: attacks the museum's motives rather than the substance of its claim
options.E: relies on a comparison between exhibits that ran under conditions too different to be compared at all

questions.answer: The museum's argument may well be weak: doubled floor space and longer hours could inflate raw first-month ticket sales independent of the exhibit's draw, so higher sales do not establish greater popularity. But pointing out that the museum's reasoning is inadequate shows only that popularity has not been proven, not that the exhibit is NOT the most popular. The critic slides from 'the argument fails' to 'this proves nothing'/the claim is unsupported in a way that treats a bad argument as a false conclusion. (A) captures this 'argument from a flawed argument' error.

questions.stem: The nutritionist's argument requires the assumption that

options.A: eating more fruit is the most effective way for office workers to improve their overall health.
options.B: workers who keep fruit bowls on their desks do not compensate by eating less fruit at home.
options.C: the workers who kept fruit bowls on their desks did not already tend to eat more fruit than other workers for reasons unrelated to the bowls.
options.D: providing desktop fruit bowls costs employers less than other workplace wellness initiatives.
options.E: every office worker prefers fresh fruit to other available snacks.

questions.answer: The nutritionist treats a correlation (bowl-keepers eat more fruit) as evidence that the bowls CAUSE more eating, then recommends giving bowls to everyone. This causal leap requires that the bowl-keepers were not already heavier fruit-eaters for some independent reason (e.g., they are health-conscious people who would eat lots of fruit anyway). If that confound holds, providing bowls to indifferent employees need not raise their consumption. Negating C - the bowl-keepers already ate more fruit for unrelated reasons - dissolves the causal inference, so C is necessary.

questions.stem: The archaeologist's conclusion depends on which one of the following assumptions?

options.A: The inland communities valued goods that the coastal community was able to produce.
options.B: The decorative patterns on the pottery were difficult to produce without specialized training.
options.C: The coastal residents did not themselves independently develop the same decorative patterns.
options.D: Trade between coastal and inland communities was common throughout the region during that period.
options.E: The pottery found at the coastal site was more finely made than pottery produced locally at the coast.

questions.answer: The argument infers regular trade from the fact that the coastal pottery matches a style found only inland. This inference assumes the matching style actually originated inland and traveled to the coast - i.e., that the coastal people did not independently invent the same patterns. If the coastal residents developed the identical patterns on their own, the shared style is no evidence of trade at all. Negating C - the coastal people independently developed the patterns - removes the only link between the shards and inland contact, so C is necessary.

questions.stem: The editorial's argument requires assuming which one of the following?

options.A: The electricity savings from rooftop solar panels will increase as electricity prices rise in the future.
options.B: No alternative renewable energy source would save new homeowners more money than rooftop solar panels.
options.C: Most people who buy new homes are concerned primarily with minimizing their long-term costs.
options.D: The added purchase price of the panels does not impose costs on new homeowners that outweigh the electricity savings.
options.E: Homeowners who install rooftop solar panels use no more electricity than homeowners who do not.

questions.answer: The editorial compares lifetime electricity savings against the panels' installation price and concludes a net financial benefit. But the higher purchase price can carry additional financial costs beyond the sticker amount - notably higher mortgage interest, property taxes, or financing charges on the larger loan. The argument needs these added costs not to exceed the savings. Negating D - the price increase imposes costs (e.g., interest) that outweigh the savings - makes the homeowner worse off and destroys the 'benefit financially' conclusion. So D is necessary.

questions.stem: The manager's reasoning depends on the assumption that

options.A: the increase in completed projects was not caused by some factor other than the switch to private offices.
options.B: private offices are the single most effective way to increase employee productivity.
options.C: employees at the other branches dislike working in open-plan offices.
options.D: the cost of converting the other branches to private offices will be recovered through higher productivity.
options.E: every employee at this branch completed more projects after the switch to private offices.

questions.answer: The manager observes a productivity rise after introducing private offices and concludes the offices caused it. This post-hoc causal claim requires ruling out other explanations for the 20 percent jump (new hires, a software upgrade, seasonal demand, etc.). If some other factor caused the increase, private offices did not 'plainly' make people more productive and the recommendation loses its basis. Negating A - another factor caused the rise - directly defeats the argument, so A is necessary.

questions.stem: The critic's argument requires the assumption that

options.A: the novelist's earlier books were not also supported by expensive marketing campaigns.
options.B: the quality of a novel is the only factor that can ever influence its sales.
options.C: the marketing campaign for the latest book was not by itself sufficient to produce the strong sales.
options.D: the reviewers who credited the marketing campaign had not actually read the novelist's latest book.
options.E: readers who buy a novelist's books are generally able to judge which of her books is the finest.

questions.answer: The critic concedes strong sales and argues the cause is the book's superior quality rather than the marketing campaign. To maintain that quality is 'the real reason,' the critic must deny that the marketing alone would have produced these sales; otherwise the rival explanation fully accounts for the result and quality need not be the cause. Negating C - the campaign by itself was sufficient to generate the strong sales - lets the marketing explanation stand on its own and undercuts the critic's claim that quality is the real reason. So C is necessary.

questions.stem: The conclusion of the columnist's argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

options.A: Sorting waste into the correct bins requires more effort than discarding everything together.
options.B: If residents sort their waste correctly, the recycling program will succeed.
options.C: The recycling program will succeed only if it requires no more effort from residents than the previous waste system did.
options.D: Some residents are unwilling to expend any extra effort on waste disposal.
options.E: No municipal program succeeds unless it requires minimal effort from residents.

questions.answer: Diagram the argument. Premise 1: Succeed -> Sort correctly. Premise 2: Sort correctly -> No more effort than discarding together. Conclusion: Not succeed. To reach 'not succeed,' we need to deny the necessary condition for success. Chaining the premises: Succeed -> Sort correctly -> No more effort. So if sorting actually DOES require more effort than discarding together (i.e., the 'no more effort' condition fails), then by contraposition residents won't sort correctly, and therefore the program won't succeed. Choice A asserts exactly that sorting requires more effort than discarding everything together. This denies the necessary condition at the end of the chain, forcing 'not sort correctly,' which forces 'not succeed.' That guarantees the conclusion.

questions.stem: The conclusion of the economist's argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

options.A: Lurensia's share of global exports declined last year.
options.B: Whenever a country's share of global exports declines, its manufacturers lay off workers.
options.C: A country's manufacturers lay off workers only if its share of global exports declines.
options.D: If Lurensia's productivity had grown faster, its export prices would not have risen.
options.E: Countries that raise their minimum wages typically experience declining export shares.

questions.answer: Chain the premises. Premise 1: Raise wage faster than productivity -> export prices rise relative to partners. Premise 2: Export prices rise relative to partners -> export share declines. Given fact: Lurensia raised wage faster than productivity. So we can derive: Lurensia's export share will decline. The conclusion is about something new: manufacturers will LAY OFF workers. Nothing in the premises connects declining export share to layoffs. Choice B provides the needed bridge: whenever export share declines, manufacturers lay off workers (decline -> layoffs). Applying B to the derived 'Lurensia's share declines' yields 'Lurensia's manufacturers lay off workers,' guaranteeing the conclusion.

questions.stem: The neurologist's conclusion follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

options.A: Any patient who begins physical therapy within 48 hours of this type of stroke and whose therapy is supervised by a licensed specialist will recover full mobility.
options.B: Mr. Okafor's physical therapy is supervised by a licensed specialist.
options.C: Every patient whose therapy is supervised by a licensed specialist recovers full mobility.
options.D: Patients who do not begin physical therapy within 48 hours of this type of stroke do not recover full mobility.
options.E: Mr. Okafor began physical therapy soon enough to have a chance at full recovery.

questions.answer: The premise gives a NECESSARY condition for full recovery: recover full mobility -> began therapy within 48 hours. The argument tries to use 'began within 48 hours' (true of Mr. Okafor, at 30 hours) plus the proviso 'therapy supervised by a licensed specialist' to conclude he WILL recover. To guarantee a positive prediction, we need a SUFFICIENT condition for full recovery. Choice A supplies it: began within 48 hours AND supervised by a specialist -> recover full mobility. Mr. Okafor began within 48 hours (30 hours), and the conclusion is conditioned on the specialist proviso, so A's antecedent is satisfied and the recovery conclusion is guaranteed.

questions.stem: The conclusion of the editorial follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

options.A: Long-term residents who run successful businesses and pay taxes are contributing members of society.
options.B: Any policy that excludes contributing members of society is unjustified.
options.C: A language requirement is justified only if it includes all long-term residents.
options.D: Some long-term residents who would be denied citizenship are not contributing members of society.
options.E: If a requirement does not exclude contributing members of society, then it is justified.

questions.answer: Premise: Justified -> does not exclude contributing members (equivalently, if it excludes a contributing member, it is not justified). Premise: the requirement would deny citizenship to long-term residents who run successful businesses and pay taxes. Conclusion: not justified. To trigger the necessary condition's contrapositive, we must establish that the requirement DOES exclude a contributing member of society. The argument describes the excluded people as business-running taxpayers but never labels them 'contributing members of society.' Choice A makes that identification: these long-term residents ARE contributing members. Then the requirement excludes a contributing member, so by the premise it is not justified. A guarantees the conclusion.

questions.stem: The conclusion of the software lead's argument follows logically if which one of the following is assumed?

options.A: If the release will not be on time, then the team should announce a delay to customers now.
options.B: If the external auditor returns her report by Wednesday, the release will be on time.
options.C: The release will be on time only if the external auditor returns her report by Wednesday.
options.D: The team should announce a delay to customers now only if the release will not be on time.
options.E: The authentication module will not pass all security audits before Friday.

questions.answer: Diagram. Premise 1: On time -> audits passed before Friday. Premise 2: Audits passed before Friday -> auditor returns report by Wednesday. Fact: auditor will NOT return report by Wednesday (she returns it Monday, next week). By Premise 2's contrapositive: not-by-Wednesday -> audits not passed before Friday. By Premise 1's contrapositive: audits not passed before Friday -> not on time. So we validly derive 'the release will NOT be on time.' The conclusion, however, is the action recommendation 'announce a delay now.' Nothing yet links 'not on time' to 'should announce a delay.' Choice A supplies that bridge: not on time -> should announce a delay now. Combined with the derived 'not on time,' A guarantees the recommendation.

questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must also be true?

options.A: Some recipes that originated in the coastal provinces cannot be prepared in under twenty minutes.
options.B: Every recipe in the collection that calls for cardamom also calls for saffron.
options.C: Any recipe in the collection that can be prepared in under twenty minutes originated in the coastal provinces.
options.D: Most recipes in the collection that call for cardamom originated in the coastal provinces.
options.E: No recipe that originated in the coastal provinces calls for cardamom.

questions.answer: Chain the statements. Some saffron recipes originated in the coastal provinces (existential). Every saffron recipe calls for cardamom (universal), so those particular coastal-province recipes call for cardamom. No cardamom recipe can be prepared in under twenty minutes, so those coastal-province recipes cannot be prepared in under twenty minutes. Therefore SOME recipes that originated in the coastal provinces cannot be prepared in under twenty minutes. The existential 'some' carries through both universal links, so (A) must be true.

questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following must be true of the Maple Street bridge?

options.A: It is not rated structurally deficient.
options.B: It is rated structurally deficient but was overlooked.
options.C: It is scheduled for inspection this year.
options.D: It carries fewer vehicles than some bridge that received priority funding.
options.E: It will be rated structurally deficient next year.

questions.answer: From the second rule: any bridge scheduled for inspection this year AND carrying more than 10,000 vehicles per day receives priority funding. Maple Street carries more than 10,000 vehicles per day but does NOT receive priority funding. By contraposition, since it meets the traffic condition but fails the conclusion, it must NOT be scheduled for inspection this year. From the first rule, structurally deficient bridges are scheduled for inspection this year; since Maple Street is not scheduled for inspection this year, by contraposition it is not structurally deficient. So (A) must be true.

questions.stem: Which one of the following can be properly inferred from the statements above?

options.A: No orchid that bloomed in March was placed in the north wing.
options.B: Every orchid given the new fertilizer bloomed in March.
options.C: Any orchid in the north wing bloomed in March.
options.D: Some orchids watered with rainwater were placed in the north wing.
options.E: Every orchid not given the new fertilizer was placed in the north wing.

questions.answer: Chain the universals: bloomed in March implies watered with rainwater; watered with rainwater implies given the new fertilizer; given the new fertilizer implies NOT in the north wing. Linking these, any orchid that bloomed in March was given the new fertilizer and therefore was not placed in the north wing. So no March-blooming orchid was in the north wing, which is (A).

questions.stem: If the statements above are true, which one of the following could be false?

options.A: Some proposals submitted by registered nonprofits were not reviewed by the junior committee.
options.B: Some proposals approved by the foundation last year requested more than one million dollars.
options.C: Every proposal the foundation approved last year was submitted by a registered nonprofit.
options.D: No proposal requesting more than one million dollars and reviewed by the junior committee exists.
options.E: Some proposals that requested more than one million dollars were submitted by registered nonprofits.
