questions.answer: The stem asks which one COULD be false (the other four must be true). (B) claims some approved proposals requested over one million dollars. The stimulus says some nonprofit proposals requested over one million, and all approved proposals were from nonprofits, but it does NOT establish that any approved proposal is among the over-one-million group. The over-one-million nonprofit proposals might all be unapproved. So (B) is not forced and could be false. By contrast: (A) follows because some nonprofit proposals exceeded one million and none of those reached the junior committee, so some nonprofit proposals were not reviewed by it; (C) merely restates a given; (D) restates the third premise; (E) is the valid 'some' with terms reordered from the second premise.

questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most helps to justify Maria's decision?

options.A: When an unforeseeable event prevents a transaction from being completed, the losses that result should be divided between the parties in proportion to the costs each has already irrevocably incurred.
options.B: A business owner should never refund money for goods that have already been produced according to a customer's specifications.
options.C: When neither party to an agreement is at fault for its disruption, and one party has already incurred unrecoverable costs in reliance on it, neither party should be made to bear the entire resulting loss alone.
options.D: A customer who cancels an order for reasons beyond her control is entitled to a full refund of any money paid.
options.E: A seller who acts in good faith is entitled to keep the full amount a customer has paid, regardless of whether the transaction is completed.

questions.answer: Maria's two stated reasons are (i) the customer should not bear the entire loss of an unforeseeable event, and (ii) Maria should not absorb costs she incurred in good faith. A justifying principle must support splitting the loss so that NEITHER party bears all of it, precisely when no one is at fault and one side has sunk unrecoverable costs. Choice C captures exactly this structure: no fault + reliance costs already incurred => neither party bears the whole loss. That licenses the partial (half) refund, which is what Maria did.

questions.stem: The columnist's reasoning most closely conforms to which one of the following principles?

options.A: A public policy should be retained only if it produces no significant drawbacks of any kind.
options.B: A practice that has both benefits and drawbacks should be evaluated by weighing the magnitude of its benefits against the magnitude of its drawbacks, rather than by the mere existence of drawbacks.
options.C: Aesthetic considerations should never be allowed to override the financial interests of low-income citizens.
options.D: A city council should reject any proposal that would reduce funding for programs serving low-income residents.
options.E: Public transportation should be funded primarily through advertising rather than through fares.

questions.answer: The columnist explicitly reframes the issue: not whether ads have drawbacks, but whether benefits outweigh harms. He then concludes the benefit (low-income fare subsidies) outweighs the drawbacks (aesthetics, distraction). This is a straightforward cost-benefit weighing principle. Choice B states exactly that: judge a practice with mixed effects by comparing the MAGNITUDE of benefits and drawbacks, not by the mere existence of drawbacks. That is the general rule the columnist applies.

questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if accepted, most justifies the editor's decision to uphold the retraction?

options.A: A scientific paper should be retracted only when its central conclusion is shown to be false.
options.B: Researchers should present their data using whatever visual techniques make the underlying trends easiest for readers to understand.
options.C: The integrity of a scientific publication depends on the accuracy of how its evidence is presented, independent of whether its conclusions happen to be correct.
options.D: A paper whose figures have been altered should be corrected rather than retracted if the alterations were not intended to deceive.
options.E: Any researcher found to have altered a figure should be permanently barred from publishing in the journal.

questions.answer: The editor says the author's defense (that the conclusion is still supported) 'missed the point entirely.' The point being missed must be that retraction turns on the integrity of how evidence is PRESENTED, not on whether the conclusion is correct. Choice C states exactly this: publication integrity depends on accurate presentation of evidence, independent of whether the conclusions are correct. That explains why the author's appeal to a still-valid conclusion is beside the point and why retraction stands.

questions.stem: Which one of the following principles, if valid, most strongly supports the analyst's evaluation of the two towns?

options.A: A scarce medical resource should be distributed so as to give every person an equal opportunity to receive it.
options.B: When a limited resource can be used to avert serious harm, it should be allocated to those for whom it will avert the greatest harm.
options.C: Public health authorities should always prioritize the elderly over younger residents in distributing medical care.
options.D: A distribution method is fair only if it treats all members of a community identically.
options.E: Towns facing a shortage of a medical resource should coordinate their distribution policies with neighboring towns.

questions.answer: The analyst praises the allocation that targets those most likely to die (greatest harm averted) and criticizes the equal-chance lottery, citing the goal of preventing 'as much serious harm as possible.' The supporting principle must make harm-minimization the criterion. Choice B does exactly that: allocate a scarce resource to those for whom it averts the GREATEST harm. This both endorses Oakdale and condemns Riverton's equal-chance method.

questions.stem: The editorial's argument most closely conforms to which one of the following principles?

options.A: A university requirement is justified whenever a majority of students do not object to it.
options.B: An institutional requirement is justified if it advances the central purpose of the institution, even at the cost of some inconvenience to those it affects.
options.C: Students should not be required to take courses that delay their progress toward a degree.
options.D: The inconvenience a requirement imposes on students is irrelevant to whether the requirement should be adopted.
options.E: A university should design its curriculum to maximize students' career prospects.

questions.answer: The editorial defines the university's purpose (producing broadly capable graduates), notes the requirement serves that purpose, and concludes the requirement is justified despite some inconvenience. The general principle being applied is: a requirement is justified if it advances the institution's central/defining purpose, even at the cost of some inconvenience. Choice B states precisely this conditional and matches the argument's structure and its explicit 'even if it imposes some inconvenience' concession.

questions.stem: Which one of the following principles is most clearly illustrated by the game designer's reasoning?

options.A: A product should be redesigned whenever a significant number of its users complain about a feature.
options.B: When a feature that causes user frustration is also the source of a product's value, the remedy should preserve that feature while reducing the frustration's unfairness, rather than eliminating the feature.
options.C: A game's difficulty should be reduced whenever players find it too punishing.
options.D: The most important goal in designing a game is to minimize the frustration players experience.
options.E: Players should be allowed to reverse any decision that leads to an outcome they did not anticipate.

questions.answer: The designer identifies that the frustrating feature (irreversible decisions) is also the source of the game's value (its rewarding tension). He rejects eliminating it (the undo proposal) and instead proposes keeping the feature while making losses feel earned rather than arbitrary, i.e., reducing the unfairness/frustration without removing the stakes. Choice B generalizes this exactly: when a frustration-causing feature is also the source of value, preserve it but reduce the frustration's unfairness rather than eliminate it.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy described above?

options.A: During the evening hours, the library employs fewer staff members at the checkout desk than it does during daytime hours.
options.B: Most of the patrons drawn in by the new evening hours came to use the library's public computers and quiet study spaces rather than to borrow books.
options.C: The library's collection of borrowable books was slightly larger last year than it had been the previous year.
options.D: A neighboring town's library reported an increase in book checkouts over the same twelve-month period.
options.E: Many of Harwick's residents prefer to read electronic books, which they download from home rather than at the library.

questions.answer: The paradox is that evening visits rose but total checkouts fell. The credited answer must explain how more visitors could coincide with fewer borrowed books. (B) does exactly this: the surge of new evening visitors came for computers and study space, not borrowing. So the extra foot traffic did not translate into checkouts, and meanwhile total checkouts could fall for other reasons (e.g., daytime borrowing patterns) without contradiction. (B) breaks the assumed link between 'more visitors' and 'more checkouts,' which is the heart of the puzzle.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent conflict between the observational finding and the experimental result?

options.A: People who habitually eat breakfast also tend to exercise more and eat more vegetables than people who skip breakfast, and these other habits are what keep their weight lower.
options.B: The participants assigned to start eating breakfast reported enjoying their breakfasts.
options.C: In the controlled study, the breakfast provided to participants was lower in calories than a typical restaurant breakfast.
options.D: Adults who skip breakfast often report feeling hungrier in the late morning than adults who eat breakfast.
options.E: The comparison group that continued to skip breakfast gained a small amount of weight over the six months.

questions.answer: The observational data link breakfast-eating to lower weight; the experiment shows that ADDING breakfast does not lower weight. These both hold if breakfast-eating is merely a marker of a healthier lifestyle rather than a cause of lower weight. (A) supplies exactly that: habitual breakfast-eaters also exercise more and eat more vegetables, and those are the real causes of their lower weight. So the correlation is genuine (eaters do weigh less) AND the intervention fails (just eating breakfast, without the other habits, does nothing). This dissolves the conflict by identifying a confounder.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to explain why the new model does not last longer on a single charge?

options.A: The new model's battery takes longer to recharge fully than the previous model's battery did.
options.B: The new model includes an always-on background feature, absent from the previous model, that continuously draws a significant amount of power.
options.C: Reviewers tested the new model under the same conditions they had used to test the previous model.
options.D: The previous model had already been praised for its exceptionally long battery life.
options.E: The new model is slightly heavier than the previous model because of its larger battery.

questions.answer: The puzzle: a bigger battery plus components that draw no more power, yet no longer runtime. Runtime depends on total energy stored divided by total power drawn. The stimulus controlled the listed components, but it did not rule out a NEW power draw. (B) introduces exactly that: an always-on background feature absent before now drains significant power continuously. This extra consumption can offset the 20 percent larger battery, so runtime stays flat while every claim in the stimulus remains true. It pinpoints an additional drain not covered by 'screen, processor, and other components.'

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent paradox?

options.A: The express bus line was funded primarily through a regional transportation grant rather than local taxes.
options.B: Once the highway became somewhat less crowded after the bus line opened, drivers who had previously avoided the highway during rush hour began using it again.
options.C: The express buses travel on a dedicated lane separate from regular highway traffic.
options.D: Surveys showed that express bus riders were highly satisfied with the speed and reliability of their commute.
options.E: Congestion on roads in the western part of the city increased over the same period.

questions.answer: The paradox: many car commuters moved to the bus, which should free up the highway, yet congestion is unchanged. (B) resolves it through induced demand: as the bus pulled cars off the highway and traffic eased slightly, previously deterred drivers who had been avoiding rush-hour driving returned to the highway, filling the freed-up space. So both facts hold: former car commuters genuinely switched to the bus, AND congestion stayed level because new drivers backfilled the capacity. This is the classic latent-demand resolution.

questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy in the editor's observations?

options.A: The magazine's long-form articles had been more expensive to produce than the new short posts are.
options.B: Since the switch, each visitor now reads many more posts per visit than before, so that total reading time per visitor has risen even though time per post has fallen.
options.C: The magazine's competitors have also begun publishing shorter posts.
options.D: Visitors who read short posts are more likely to share them on social media than visitors who read long-form articles were.
options.E: The number of distinct visitors to the site each day has remained roughly constant since the switch.

questions.answer: The puzzle: time spent per single post fell, yet total daily time on the site rose. These reconcile if visitors now consume MANY more posts per visit. (B) states exactly that: lower time per post, but far more posts read, so per-visitor time (and thus total site time) increases. The two facts coexist because the per-unit metric and the aggregate metric move in opposite directions for a clear arithmetic reason. This directly bridges the 'per post down' and 'total up' figures.

questions.stem: Dalton and Priya disagree over whether

options.A: the city's diesel buses emit pollutants
options.B: downtown air quality has declined over the past decade
options.C: replacing the diesel buses with electric buses would meaningfully improve downtown air quality
options.D: the industrial zone to the west is the largest single source of downtown pollution
options.E: the city should reduce pollution from the industrial zone

questions.answer: A point at issue must be something one speaker affirms and the other denies. Dalton's whole argument is that replacing diesel buses with electric ones is worth doing because the buses pollute and air quality has declined - he is asserting the switch would help. Priya explicitly says 'switching to electric buses won't help our downtown air,' directly denying that the switch would meaningfully improve air quality. That is exactly choice C: Dalton affirms it, Priya denies it.

questions.stem: The two reviewers are committed to disagreeing about which one of the following?

options.A: whether the novel is engrossing
options.B: whether the novel's prose is vivid and cinematic
options.C: whether the unreliable narrator is what makes the novel engrossing
options.D: whether unreliable narrators are generally a gimmick in fiction
options.E: whether the reader must reconstruct the real story while reading the novel

questions.answer: Reviewer 1 asserts that the unreliable narrator 'is the source of its power' - i.e., the thing that makes the book engrossing. Reviewer 2 directly denies this: the unreliable narrator 'adds nothing,' and the prose is 'what truly grips the reader,' adding that a reliable narrator would have been 'just as engrossing.' So Reviewer 1 affirms and Reviewer 2 denies that the unreliable narrator is what makes the novel engrossing. That is choice C.

questions.stem: Marcus and Lena disagree about whether

options.A: the company's employees would be happier under a four-day workweek
options.B: the existing studies provide good reason to expect that our company's output would stay the same under a four-day workweek
options.C: a four-day workweek has ever succeeded at any firm
options.D: the company is currently well managed
options.E: employee happiness is a legitimate goal for the company to pursue

questions.answer: Marcus relies on the studies as evidence that 'we would lose nothing in output' - i.e., the studies give us good reason to expect our output would hold. Lena's reply targets exactly this inference: the studies are 'misleading' because the trial firms were unrepresentative, so 'we can't assume our output would hold steady.' Marcus affirms the studies support the prediction for our firm; Lena denies it. That is choice B.

questions.stem: The dialogue most strongly supports the claim that the health official and the traffic researcher disagree about whether

options.A: most drivers already know that texting while driving is dangerous
options.B: texting while driving is in fact dangerous
options.C: a public awareness campaign could reduce texting while driving
options.D: people sometimes engage in behavior they know to be risky
options.E: reducing texting while driving is a worthwhile public goal

questions.answer: The official argues a campaign 'would change no behavior' because everyone already knows the risk - so a campaign cannot reduce the behavior. The researcher counters that 'a well-designed campaign ... could reduce texting while driving even among those who already know the risks.' The official denies a campaign could reduce the behavior; the researcher affirms it could. That is choice C.

questions.stem: The architect and the planner disagree over whether

options.A: adding a protected bike lane increases the number of cyclists on a street
options.B: cities should try to reduce car traffic
options.C: the increase in cyclists after a bike lane is added consists mainly of former drivers
options.D: the increase in cyclists that follows adding a bike lane reflects a reduction in car trips
options.E: some new cyclists are people who previously took the bus

questions.answer: The architect infers from the rise in cyclists that 'fewer of those trips are being made by car' - the increase reflects replaced car trips. The planner denies exactly this inference: 'The rise in cyclists doesn't show that car trips are being replaced,' and 'it doesn't follow that it takes cars off the road.' The architect affirms and the planner denies that the cyclist increase reflects a reduction in car trips. That is choice D.

questions.stem: The point at issue between the curator and the historian is whether

options.A: the painting was created during Vermeer's lifetime
options.B: the evidence cited establishes that Vermeer painted the work
options.C: the pigments in the painting were available in the Netherlands during Vermeer's lifetime
options.D: any of Vermeer's contemporaries was as skilled as Vermeer
options.E: the painting is a valuable work of art

questions.answer: The curator argues the evidence - matching light technique plus period-appropriate pigments - warrants attributing the painting to Vermeer. The historian denies that this evidence does that work: the analysis 'proves only that the painting could date from Vermeer's era, not that he painted it,' and the evidence 'is consistent with the painting being by another Dutch artist.' The curator affirms the cited evidence establishes Vermeer's authorship; the historian denies it. That is choice B.

questions.stem: The flawed reasoning in the argument above is most similar to that in which one of the following?

options.A: All of the apples in the crate that were bruised were thrown out. This apple was thrown out. Therefore, this apple was bruised.
options.B: Each book that the library digitized is available online. This book is available online. Therefore, the library must have digitized many books.
options.C: Everyone who attended the seminar received a certificate. Paulo did not receive a certificate. Therefore, Paulo did not attend the seminar.
options.D: All the runners who finished the marathon qualified for the regional meet. Lena qualified for the regional meet, so Lena finished the marathon and trained hard.
options.E: Most of the volunteers who signed up early were assigned to the front desk. Devi signed up early, so Devi was probably assigned to the front desk.

questions.answer: The stimulus has the form: All who have property P have property Q (studied -> passed). X has Q (Mara passed). Therefore X has P (Mara studied). This affirms the consequent / illicitly converts the conditional. Choice A reproduces this exactly: All bruised apples were thrown out (bruised -> thrown out); this apple was thrown out (has Q); therefore it was bruised (has P). Same affirming-the-consequent flaw, same number of terms, same scope (universal 'all'), same single conclusion about one individual.

questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

options.A: If the orchard is pruned, the trees will yield more fruit. If the trees yield more fruit, the cooperative's profits will grow. The cooperative's profits did grow. Therefore, the orchard was pruned.
options.B: If the bakery lowers its prices, foot traffic will increase. If foot traffic increases, the bakery will need more staff. The bakery has lowered its prices. So the bakery will need more staff.
options.C: If the museum extends its hours, attendance will rise. If attendance rises, donations will increase. The museum did not extend its hours. Therefore, donations will not increase.
options.D: If the team practices daily, its passing will improve. The team's passing improved. Therefore, the team practiced daily and its defense improved as well.
options.E: Either the company expands overseas or it merges with a rival. If it expands overseas, revenue will climb. The company did not merge with a rival. Therefore, revenue will climb.

questions.answer: The stimulus chains two conditionals and then applies the antecedent of the first to reach the consequent of the second: A->B, B->C, A is true, therefore C. This is valid hypothetical syllogism plus modus ponens. Choice B has exactly this form: lowers prices -> foot traffic increases, foot traffic increases -> needs more staff, bakery lowered prices, therefore needs more staff. Same chained conditionals, same affirmation of the first antecedent, same valid conclusion.

questions.stem: The reasoning in which one of the following is most closely parallel to that in the argument above?

options.A: Either the painting was damaged in transit or it was damaged in storage. If it had been damaged in transit, the crate would show dents. The crate shows no dents. Therefore, the painting was damaged in storage.
options.B: Either the alarm failed or the battery died. If the battery had died, the indicator light would be off. The indicator light is off. Therefore, the battery died.
options.C: If the manuscript was edited in-house, it contains the house style marks. It does contain those marks. So it was edited in-house, not by a freelancer.
options.D: Either the shipment is late or the tracking system is wrong. The shipment is not late. If the tracking system were wrong, customers would have complained, and many have. Therefore, the tracking system is wrong.
options.E: Either Dana or Ravi closed the store. If Dana closed the store, the lights would be off. The lights are off, so Dana closed the store and set the alarm.

questions.answer: The stimulus form: Either P or Q. If Q, then R. Not R (R is false). Therefore P. It uses a disjunction, then eliminates one disjunct by modus tollens on a conditional tied to that disjunct, concluding the other disjunct. Choice A matches exactly: Either transit or storage; if transit, then dents; no dents (modus tollens eliminates transit); therefore storage. Same disjunctive syllogism completed by ruling out one option through denied consequent.

questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits a flawed pattern of reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?

options.A: A film is worth watching only if it has a coherent plot. This documentary has a coherent plot. Therefore, this documentary is worth watching.
options.B: A bridge is safe only if it passes inspection. This bridge did not pass inspection. Therefore, this bridge is not safe.
options.C: A candidate will be hired only if she interviews well. This candidate interviewed well and has strong references. Therefore, she will be hired.
options.D: A restaurant succeeds only if it has good food. This restaurant has good food and a prime location. Therefore, it will surely succeed.
options.E: A plant thrives only if it gets sunlight. This plant is thriving. Therefore, it must be getting sunlight.

questions.answer: The stimulus mistakes a NECESSARY condition for a SUFFICIENT one. 'Worth prescribing only if benefits outweigh side effects' means worth-prescribing -> benefits-outweigh (the outweighing is necessary, not sufficient). The argument then asserts the necessary condition is met and concludes the medication is worth prescribing, treating a necessary condition as sufficient. Choice A commits the identical error: 'worth watching only if coherent plot' (necessary), the plot is coherent, therefore worth watching. Same single necessary condition affirmed and wrongly treated as sufficient, with one clean conclusion.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the blood of the horseshoe crab is blue because of

options.A: the presence of amebocytes that clot when exposed to bacterial toxins
options.B: a copper-based oxygen carrier called hemocyanin
options.C: the animal's close evolutionary relationship to spiders and scorpions
options.D: the thirty percent of blood drawn during pharmaceutical harvesting
options.E: the absence of any synthetic substitute with regulatory acceptance

questions.answer: The passage states the blood 'is blue owing to a copper-based oxygen carrier called hemocyanin.' The phrase 'owing to' directly attributes the blue color to hemocyanin, making B the explicitly supported answer.

questions.stem: The passage states which one of the following about the medieval Icelandic legal system?

options.A: The Lawspeaker was elected by the injured parties who brought cases to the Althing.
options.B: Outlawry was the only punishment available to the Althing for serious offenses.
options.C: The responsibility for enforcing a verdict fell to the injured party or his kin.
options.D: The system collapsed because it lacked a written legal code.
options.E: Norwegian rule was invited by parties who had been declared outlaws.

questions.answer: The passage explicitly says an injured party, 'or his kin, bore responsibility for bringing a case and, if successful, for enforcing the verdict.' C restates this directly.

questions.stem: According to the passage, fluorescence differs from phosphorescence in that fluorescence

options.A: stores absorbed energy and releases it over a period of hours
options.B: involves electrons trapped in a 'forbidden' higher-energy state
options.C: ceases within nanoseconds after the energy source is removed
options.D: is not a form of photoluminescence
options.E: produces a fainter light when engineered for greater endurance

questions.answer: The passage states that in fluorescence, 'once the energy source is removed, the glow ceases within nanoseconds.' C directly captures this distinguishing feature of fluorescence.

questions.stem: The passage asserts which one of the following about the Voynich manuscript?

options.A: Radiocarbon dating established that the text was written in the early fifteenth century.
options.B: The plants depicted in its illustrations have not been matched to any known species.
options.C: Statistical analysis has proven that the script encodes a real language.
options.D: The manuscript has resisted decipherment because it is a hoax.
options.E: The manuscript consists of roughly 240 astronomical diagrams.

questions.answer: The passage states the manuscript is illustrated with 'drawings of plants, none of which has been matched to a known species.' B restates this explicit claim.

questions.stem: According to the passage, coffee leaf rust damages coffee plants by

options.A: infecting the berries and rendering them unharvestable
options.B: causing premature leaf drop that starves the plant
options.C: lowering the flavor quality of Arabica varieties
options.D: spreading orange spores that warm the surrounding air
options.E: forcing growers to abandon high-altitude plantations

questions.answer: The passage states the fungus covers leaf undersides with spores 'causing premature leaf drop that starves the plant.' B captures the explicit mechanism of damage.

questions.stem: The passage states which one of the following about the 1883 adoption of time zones in North America?

options.A: It was mandated by the United States government through the Standard Time Act.
options.B: It was undertaken by railway companies acting on their own initiative.
options.C: It was accepted immediately and without resistance by municipalities.
options.D: It caused local solar time to shift by a minute for every twelve miles.
options.E: It was prompted by a government effort to codify natural time into law.

questions.answer: The passage states that in 1883 railway companies acted 'on their own initiative rather than by government mandate' to divide the continent into time zones. B restates this explicitly.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

options.A: Protected wilderness areas have generally failed to preserve the species they were designed to protect.
options.B: Indigenous practices such as controlled burning and selective harvesting were the sole cause of high species richness in certain landscapes.
options.C: The conservation ideal of untouched nature may be flawed because some prized ecosystems were in fact sustained by long-standing human activity.
options.D: Conservation biologists should abandon the practice of establishing protected reserves in favor of restoring indigenous land-management techniques.
options.E: Species richness in long-protected reserves has declined because the reserves were too small to support viable populations.

questions.answer: The passage builds toward its final sentence, which states that the ideal of untouched nature 'may rest on a misreading' of how prized ecosystems arose. Choice C captures exactly this thesis: the cherished ideal is questionable because some valued ecosystems were actually maintained by human activity. It has the correct scope (a qualified challenge to an assumption) and the correct hedge ('may'), mirroring the author's 'may suggest' framing.

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

options.A: Music notation is unnecessary for the performance of complex polyphonic music.
options.B: Oral musical traditions have produced polyphony at least as sophisticated as that of notated traditions.
options.C: Contrary to the conventional view, musical complexity tended to drive the development of notation rather than the reverse.
options.D: Medieval European notation systems developed only after their corresponding musical practices were established.
options.E: Music historians have systematically misunderstood the role of oral traditions in the history of polyphony.

questions.answer: The passage explicitly states in its final sentence that 'the familiar claim thus inverts the actual relationship,' and that complexity created the demand for notation rather than notation enabling complexity. Choice C states precisely this reversal of the conventional causal claim, with correct scope and the appropriate 'tended to' hedge matching the passage's 'more frequently functioned.'

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the author's attitude toward the zoning reforms discussed in the passage?

options.A: qualified support tempered by skepticism about the more ambitious claims made for the reforms
options.B: wholehearted endorsement of the reforms and the affordability outcomes their advocates predict
options.C: settled opposition to the reforms on the ground that they benefit only upper-income buyers
options.D: detached neutrality, presenting competing positions without favoring either
options.E: alarm that the reforms will worsen the very housing shortages they were meant to address

questions.answer: The author twice affirms value in the reforms ('no question that such reforms can ease the housing shortages'; 'A useful tool oversold is still a useful tool') while directing criticism specifically at the 'more sweeping claims' and the framing of zoning as a 'sufficient cure.' That combination of genuine support plus a narrowly targeted, evidence-based skepticism is exactly 'qualified support tempered by skepticism,' so (A) is the credited answer.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the principle of minimal intervention is best described as which one of the following?

options.A: appreciation of its underlying caution combined with concern that it can be applied too rigidly
options.B: admiration so complete that the author endorses declining ever to remove later additions
options.C: dismissal of the principle as a fashionable error with no sound basis
options.D: indifference, since the author regards the choice of cleaning method as purely technical
options.E: regret that earlier conservators did not adopt the principle far sooner

questions.answer: The author 'can appreciate the humility' behind minimal intervention and grants that past over-cleaning 'taught us caution at real cost,' establishing genuine respect for the principle. But the author 'confess[es] to some unease' when it 'hardens... into a near-prohibition' and argues that treating any removal as presumptuous 'mistake[s] one virtue... for the whole of the conservator's responsibility.' Respect for the rationale plus worry about rigid application is precisely (A).

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the author's attitude toward the use of nudges in policy?

options.A: outright rejection of nudges as a manipulative substitute for legitimate governance
options.B: acceptance of their value in limited settings paired with worry about overextending them
options.C: enthusiastic agreement that nudges are a low-cost solution applicable at every scale
options.D: fear that nudges, however applied, are likely to cause significant harm to citizens
options.E: purely descriptive interest in nudges, with no evaluation of their merits offered

questions.answer: The author concedes nudges have 'a real track record' 'in narrow domains' and that their appeal is 'understandable,' granting genuine value in limited settings. The reservation is targeted: the 'breezy confidence' that nudges suit 'problems of every scale' and the worry that their convenience will crowd out 'more demanding remedies.' Limited acceptance plus concern about overextension is (B).

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the recent reappraisal of oral traditions can most accurately be described as

options.A: endorsement of the reappraisal coupled with reservations about how some of its champions characterize oral tradition
options.B: nostalgia for the older view that oral traditions are charming but unreliable
options.C: unreserved celebration of the reappraisal and of every claim made by its advocates
options.D: neutrality between the older skepticism and the newer appreciation of oral sources
options.E: conviction that oral traditions should now be regarded as more reliable than written documents

questions.answer: The author says the pendulum has swung 'rightly so' and 'welcome[s] this corrective,' clearly endorsing the reappraisal. Yet he says what 'gives me pause' is the reformers' tendency to treat oral tradition as mere 'transcription by other means.' Endorsing the shift while objecting to how some champions characterize the sources is exactly (A).

questions.stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the author's attitude toward rewilding?

options.A: support for its aims combined with criticism of romanticized portrayals that misrepresent what it involves
options.B: opposition to rewilding on the ground that it inevitably conflicts with nearby residents
options.C: agreement with the popular view that rewilding lets nature heal itself once humans withdraw
options.D: impartial reporting of the debate over rewilding without taking a side
options.E: frustration that rewilding projects rely on fences and culls rather than leaving land untouched

questions.answer: The author 'share[s] much of the underlying instinct' and calls restoring ecological complexity 'a worthy aim,' supporting rewilding's goals. The criticism is aimed not at rewilding but at its 'romantic' presentation as nature 'healing itself,' which 'sets expectations that the projects cannot meet.' He closes wanting rewilding 'defended honestly.' Support for the aim plus criticism of the misleading portrayal is (A).

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the complaint that contemporary jazz is too cerebral is most accurately described as

options.A: skeptical of the complaint while conceding it contains a limited measure of truth
options.B: full agreement that contemporary jazz has sacrificed feeling for technical display
options.C: complete dismissal of the complaint as having no basis whatsoever
options.D: indifference, since the author regards musical taste as wholly subjective
options.E: confidence that today's difficult jazz will certainly be reevaluated as warm and joyful

questions.answer: The author grants 'a grain of truth' to the complaint and admits 'virtuosity can become an end in itself,' so he does not dismiss it. But he is 'wary of the broader indictment,' recalls the same charge against bebop, and 'doubt[s] that we are good judges, in the moment,' of which difficult music is hollow. Doubt about the complaint plus a limited concession is exactly (A).

questions.stem: The reference to taverns, workshops, and town squares functions primarily to

options.A: illustrate the kinds of social settings through which communal reading extended a printed text's reach beyond those who could read
options.B: establish that literacy rates in sixteenth-century Europe rose more slowly than historians had previously believed
options.C: identify the specific locations where the earliest European printing presses were installed
options.D: suggest that printed pamphlets were more influential in urban areas than in rural ones
options.E: argue that communal reading has been unfairly neglected by historians of literacy

questions.answer: The passage's thesis is that the pamphlet's influence depended on social settings of performance rather than on the number of literate readers. The list of venues is a concrete illustration of those settings, showing how one copy reached many non-readers. That illustrative, thesis-supporting role is exactly what choice A names.

questions.stem: The sentence noting that aluminum's weight savings may matter more to a racing cyclist functions primarily to

options.A: concede that steel frames are heavier than aluminum frames and therefore unsuitable for competition
options.B: qualify the discussion of fatigue by showing that the trade-off favors aluminum under certain conditions of use
options.C: prove that aluminum is the superior material for all high-performance bicycle frames
options.D: introduce a new objection that the rest of the passage goes on to refute
options.E: demonstrate that strength-to-weight ratio is an unreliable measure of any material's value

questions.answer: The passage argues that material choice depends on use, not on a single figure. After emphasizing aluminum's fatigue weakness, the author inserts the racing-cyclist sentence to prevent the reader from concluding steel is simply better. It qualifies the fatigue point by identifying a use-context where aluminum wins, which directly serves the thesis. Choice B captures this concessive, qualifying role.

questions.stem: The detail that the openings appear in the drafts as insertions squeezed into margins functions primarily to

options.A: support the claim that Vance's descriptive passages were composed after, rather than before, the rest of each chapter
options.B: suggest that Vance was a careless writer who paid little attention to revision
options.C: explain why critics in Vance's lifetime admired her descriptive openings
options.D: establish that the surviving manuscripts are incomplete and therefore unreliable
options.E: prove that Vance's descriptions are less artistically valuable than her dialogue

questions.answer: The passage's central claim is that Vance wrote her openings last, contrary to the assumption that they were generative starting points. The physical evidence of marginal insertions is offered as proof of that compositional sequence. The detail supplies textual evidence for the timing claim, which is what choice A states.

questions.stem: The discussion of the metropolitan corridor expanded from eight to twelve lanes serves primarily to

options.A: provide a concrete instance of the induced-demand phenomenon described in the preceding sentences
options.B: establish that congestion pricing is more cost-effective than highway expansion
options.C: demonstrate that no highway expansion has ever reduced congestion anywhere
options.D: explain the engineering reasons why adding lanes increases a highway's capacity
options.E: introduce the concept of induced demand for the first time in the passage

questions.answer: The passage explains induced demand in general terms, then offers the eight-to-twelve-lane corridor as a specific case in which speeds returned to pre-expansion levels. The example illustrates and corroborates the general mechanism just described. Choice A names this exemplifying function.

questions.stem: The discussion of folklore functions primarily to

options.A: offer an example supporting the critics' claim that a shared domain can stimulate creative output
options.B: prove that copyright protection should be abolished entirely
options.C: concede that authors deserve no return on their creative work
options.D: describe the historical origins of modern copyright law
options.E: establish that traditional tales are artistically superior to copyrighted works

questions.answer: The critics claim long copyright terms can stifle creation because art builds on existing material. Folklore is introduced as an 'instructive comparison' showing a domain with no ownership that nonetheless generated abundant new work. It functions as supporting evidence for the critics' position, which choice A states.

questions.stem: The statement that 'One might expect such plants to be at a disadvantage' functions primarily to

options.A: articulate the expectation that the passage's subsequent evidence overturns
options.B: present the author's considered conclusion about caffeinated nectar
options.C: summarize the experimental findings regarding bee memory
options.D: concede a flaw in the experimental methods used to study pollinators
options.E: explain why caffeine is toxic to bees at high concentrations

questions.answer: The passage sets up an apparent paradox, states the naive expectation that toxin-producing plants should suffer, and then uses experimental evidence to show the opposite. The quoted sentence voices the expectation that the rest of the paragraph reverses, framing the surprise. Choice A captures this setup-to-be-overturned function.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information in the passage?

options.A: The third fungal partner is responsible for supplying lichens with the sugars they need to survive.
options.B: Some lichens that share the same two traditionally recognized partners can nonetheless differ in outward appearance.
options.C: Lichens cannot survive in the absence of the recently discovered third fungal partner.
options.D: Biologists had no reliable means of distinguishing lichen species before the advent of genomic surveys.
options.E: The third fungal partner performs no function in the lichens in which it occurs.

questions.answer: The passage states the third partner appears in lichens that differ markedly in appearance 'even when their two traditionally recognized partners are genetically identical.' That directly entails that lichens sharing the same two recognized partners can still differ in outward appearance. This is one supported step beyond the text.

questions.stem: The transit director's statements, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?

options.A: The express bus line has reduced the total number of cars on downtown streets compared to the previous year.
options.B: Without the express bus line, downtown rush-hour traffic speeds would likely have been worse than they currently are.
options.C: The downtown workforce will continue to grow in the coming year.
options.D: The critics deliberately ignored the growth of the downtown workforce.
options.E: Express bus lines are the most effective method available for managing urban traffic congestion.

questions.answer: The director argues that the workforce grew 8% and that absent the line those new commuters would have added cars to crowded streets. Combined with the fact that speeds merely stayed flat (rather than worsening), this supports that without the line, speeds would likely have been worse than they are now. That is the modest inference the director's reasoning licenses.

questions.stem: The information in the passage most strongly supports which one of the following?

options.A: Medieval monasteries kept no records other than the account books compiled for bishops.
options.B: The figures in medieval monastic account books were sometimes shaped by considerations other than accurate record-keeping.
options.C: Tax assessments and merchants' ledgers are entirely reliable sources of information about monastic finances.
options.D: Bishops were generally unaware that the account books they received understated monastic holdings.
options.E: Medieval monks who managed daily affairs were less competent at record-keeping than the officials who prepared the reports.

questions.answer: The passage says officials had reason to present finances favorably and that the books understate holdings precisely when bishops scrutinized most closely. Together these support that the figures were sometimes shaped by considerations other than accuracy (i.e., by self-interested presentation). This is a cautious, fully supported step.

questions.stem: Which one of the following can most reasonably be inferred from the passage?

options.A: The first generation of stars dispersed heavy elements into space through a process different from ordinary supernovae.
options.B: The oldest stars observable today were themselves members of the first generation of stars.
options.C: Iron cannot be produced by any stellar process other than an ordinary supernova explosion.
options.D: Stars formed from primordial gas were less massive than stars that form today.
options.E: Ordinary supernovae are no longer occurring anywhere in the universe.

questions.answer: The passage says the first stars could not have produced ordinary supernovae, yet their chemical signatures appear in later stars, meaning they 'dispersed their material into space by some means.' The supported inference is that they dispersed material by a process other than ordinary supernovae. This combines the two stated facts in one step.

questions.stem: The economist's statements, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?

options.A: Raising the minimum wage always increases total employment.
options.B: The common argument overlooks a factor that could partly offset the effect it describes.
options.C: Low-income workers contribute more to the economy than higher-income workers do.
options.D: Employers never reduce hiring in response to higher labor costs.
options.E: Local businesses set their prices primarily on the basis of consumer demand.

questions.answer: The economist grants that higher labor costs create a cost-increase effect but argues the common argument ignores a second, opposing effect: increased spending by low-wage workers boosting demand for labor. So the common argument overlooks a factor that could partly offset the effect it identifies. That is precisely what 'depends on the balance between two opposing effects' implies.

questions.stem: The curator's statements most strongly support which one of the following?

options.A: The museum's most important obligation is to maximize the comfort and satisfaction of its current visitors.
options.B: Preserving certain works for future generations can justify a policy that reduces present visitors' enjoyment of them.
options.C: Dim lighting has no effect on visitors' ability to appreciate the paintings on display.
options.D: All of the paintings in the museum's collection are several centuries old.
options.E: The conservation staff's recommendations are always followed by the museum's curators.

questions.answer: The curator concedes the dim galleries are less striking (reducing present enjoyment) yet defends the policy because it preserves irreplaceable works for future generations, calling preservation the museum's 'most basic responsibility.' This supports that preserving works for the future can justify a policy that reduces present visitors' enjoyment. It is the curator's core position in one step.
